subject: Government
title: Military Rule and Democratic Transitions
outline: Meaning and features of military rule
Causes of military intervention in politics
Structure of military government in Nigeria
Achievements and failures of military rule
Transition programmes and the return to civil rule

modules.title: Nature and Causes of Military Rule
modules.html:
1. Features of Military Government

  1. Comes to power unconstitutionally through a coup d'etat.
  2. Suspends or modifies the constitution and dissolves elected legislatures.
  3. Rules by decree (federal) and edict (state), often with ouster clauses excluding the courts.
  4. Bans political parties and political activity.
  5. Fusion of executive and legislative powers in a supreme ruling council.
  6. Centralisation of power — federalism becomes largely nominal.
  7. Chain of command, secrecy and limited public accountability.
  8. Restriction of press freedom and human rights.

2. Causes of Military Intervention

  • Corruption and self-enrichment by politicians.
  • Electoral malpractice, rigging and post-election violence.
  • Ethnic and regional conflict threatening national unity.
  • Economic mismanagement and inflation.
  • Weak and abused institutions; disregard for the rule of law.
  • Personal ambition of officers and grievances over promotion, welfare and equipment.
  • Contagion — successful coups in neighbouring states.
  • Public disillusionment which makes intervention initially popular.

3. Structure

OrganRole
Supreme Military Council / AFRC / PRCHighest law-making and policy body
Head of State and Commander-in-ChiefChief executive, chairs the council
National Council of StatesAdvisory body of governors and senior officers
Federal Executive CouncilMinisters implementing policy
Military Governors/AdministratorsHead states, issue edicts
JudiciaryRetained but limited by ouster clauses and special tribunals

examples.q: What is an ouster clause and why is it objectionable?
examples.a: An ouster clause is a provision in a decree stating that no court shall entertain any question about the validity of the decree or of acts done under it. It is objectionable because it destroys judicial review and access to court — core elements of the rule of law — leaving citizens without remedy against detention or seizure of property, as under Decree No. 2 of 1984 which allowed detention without trial.

examples.q: Explain why coups are described as contagious in West Africa.
examples.a: A successful coup demonstrates to officers elsewhere that intervention can succeed at low cost and confers power and wealth. Shared training, borders and regional media spread both the example and the justification ('to end corruption'). This is why ECOWAS and the AU now adopt automatic suspension of member states following unconstitutional changes of government — to raise the cost and break the chain.

modules.title: Nigerian Military Regimes and the Return to Civil Rule
modules.html:
1. Chronology

PeriodHead of StateKey events
Jan–Jul 1966Maj-Gen J. T. U. Aguiyi-IronsiFirst coup of 15 Jan 1966 led by Maj. Nzeogwu; Decree No. 34 (Unification Decree) abolished federalism
1966–1975Gen. Yakubu GowonCounter-coup Jul 1966; 12 states created 1967; civil war 1967–1970; oil boom; Reconstruction, Reconciliation, Rehabilitation; NYSC 1973
1975–1976Gen. Murtala MohammedPurge of public service; 19 states (1976); Abuja chosen as capital; Local Government Reform 1976; assassinated Feb 1976
1976–1979Gen. Olusegun ObasanjoCompleted transition; 1979 Constitution; handover to Shagari 1 Oct 1979
1983–1985Maj-Gen Muhammadu BuhariWar Against Indiscipline; Decrees 2 and 4; economic austerity
1985–1993Gen. Ibrahim BabangidaSAP 1986; two-party system SDP/NRC; annulment of 12 June 1993 election; 'stepped aside' Aug 1993
Aug–Nov 1993Chief Ernest ShonekanInterim National Government, declared illegal by court
1993–1998Gen. Sani AbachaSix states created 1996 (total 36); PRC; repression; death June 1998
1998–1999Gen. Abdulsalami AbubakarRapid transition; 1999 Constitution; handover 29 May 1999

2. Achievements and Failures

Achievements: preservation of national unity after the civil war; creation of states and the 1976 local government reform; establishment of the FCT, NYSC, universities and infrastructure; indigenisation decrees; quick decision-making in emergencies; UPE (1976); ECOMOG peacekeeping.

Failures: suspension of the constitution and rights; abolition of true federalism; corruption on a large scale; repression of the press and the judiciary; annulment of the 12 June 1993 election, widely regarded as Nigeria's freest; economic hardship under SAP; erosion of professionalism in the armed forces.

3. Preventing Military Rule

  • Credible elections and genuine democratic legitimacy.
  • Good governance, accountability and anti-corruption enforcement.
  • Professional, well-equipped and well-paid armed forces confined to constitutional roles.
  • Strong institutions: independent judiciary, active legislature, free press, vibrant civil society.
  • Civic education so that citizens reject unconstitutional change.
  • Regional sanctions — the AU and ECOWAS suspension regimes.
  • Constitutional criminalisation of coups as treason.

examples.q: Why is 12 June 1993 significant in Nigerian political history?
examples.a: It was the presidential election generally judged the freest and fairest in Nigeria's history, contested by M. K. O. Abiola (SDP) and Bashir Tofa (NRC) across ethnic and religious lines. Its annulment by General Babangida triggered mass protests, the flight of investment, Abiola's later detention and death, and prolonged illegitimacy for the Abacha regime. It became the symbol of the pro-democracy struggle, and in 2018 was recognised as Democracy Day, replacing 29 May.

examples.q: Compare Decree No. 34 of 1966 with the federal structure it replaced.
examples.a: Decree No. 34, Ironsi's Unification Decree, abolished the regions and the federal structure, converted Nigeria into a unitary state with a single national civil service, and renamed regions 'groups of provinces'. Northerners read it as a design for Southern bureaucratic domination; the resulting riots and the July counter-coup made it the clearest example of how military centralisation destabilised a plural federation. It was repealed shortly afterwards.

quiz.q: Nigeria's first military coup occurred on:
quiz.solution: Major Nzeogwu and others struck on 15 January 1966, ending the First Republic.
Federal decrees and state edicts replace Acts and laws.
Ironsi's Unification Decree abolished the federal structure.

quiz.q: The Nigerian Civil War was fought between:
quiz.solution: The war lasted from July 1967 to January 1970.

quiz.q: Twelve states were created in Nigeria in:
quiz.solution: Gowon created twelve states in May 1967 on the eve of the civil war.

quiz.q: The Head of State assassinated in February 1976 was:
quiz.solution: General Murtala Mohammed was killed in the Dimka coup attempt.
Alhaji Shehu Shagari of the NPN became President on 1 October 1979.
It criminalised publications embarrassing to public officers, even if true.

quiz.q: The Structural Adjustment Programme was introduced in:
quiz.solution: Babangida adopted SAP in 1986 with currency devaluation and deregulation.

quiz.q: The 12 June 1993 election was won by:
quiz.solution: Abiola of the SDP was widely acknowledged as winner before annulment.

quiz.q: The Interim National Government was headed by:
quiz.solution: Chief Ernest Shonekan led the ING from August to November 1993.
Abacha created six additional states in October 1996.

quiz.q: An ouster clause is intended to:
quiz.solution: It bars courts from questioning decrees or acts done under them.

quiz.q: Which is an achievement of military rule in Nigeria?
quiz.solution: The uniform third-tier reform of 1976 was a lasting military-era achievement.

quiz.q: A key way to prevent military intervention is:
quiz.solution: Legitimate, accountable civilian government removes the pretext for coups.

quiz.q: Democracy Day in Nigeria was moved to 12 June in:
quiz.solution: In 2018 the date was changed to honour the annulled 1993 election.
